The October meeting of the Graphical AI Working Group focused on reviewing Dale's Schema Search RFC proposal, which introduces a new approach to complement semantic introspection for natural language to schema mapping. Dale presented the proposal for a new HTTP endpoint at /graphql/schema that would accept natural language queries and return schema slices that are valid on their own, allowing agents to construct operations without requiring multiple turns or context pollution. The group discussed implementation details including parameter naming, response formats, caching considerations, and the importance of returning a minimum valid schema that agents can use to build queries. Key feedback included using text/plain for initial responses, implementing progressive schema expansion through POST requests, and leveraging the capabilities API for discovery. The team agreed that the proposal should aim for one-shot schema retrieval to maintain effectiveness, and discussed potential integration with agent harnesses for native support.

## Summary

### GraphQL AI Working Group Meeting

The meeting began with informal introductions and casual conversation among participants including Pascal, Jeff, Dale, Mia, zkozina, and Mark. Pascal welcomed everyone to the October meeting of the GraphQL AI Working Group and outlined the agenda, which focused on the Schema Search RFC. The group agreed to the meeting guidelines including recording and use of AI summary tools, and Dale was introduced to present the main agenda item about the Schema Search RFC.

### GraphQL Schema Search Proposal

Dale presented a proposal for "schema search," a new approach to complement semantic introspection in GraphQL. He outlined plans to add a new endpoint using the GraphQL over HTTP spec, with parameters QMV (natural language query) and V (spec version), to return a valid, minimum schema slice that agents can use to construct operations. Dale also discussed handling incremental schema building through parameters like "known" or request body methods to append additional information over time.

### SDL Versioning Discussion Meeting

Pascal and Dale discussed the relevance of specifying SDL (Schema Definition Language) version in the document, with Pascal questioning the necessity of this complexity for server-side implementation. They agreed that versioning might be more appropriate at the schema level through directives rather than in the response. Pascal also suggested allowing both GET and POST methods for schema requests and noted the potential caching implications of POST requests. The discussion concluded with Pascal highlighting a new feature allowing empty field sets in inputs, particularly relevant for semantic search use cases.

### Schema Search Implementation Discussion

Pascal proposed adding example values and operations to schema annotations to help LLMs understand schema structure. Mark expressed support for directive-based implementations and discussed the importance of having different tiers of support for schema search functionality. Dale confirmed that the current specification intentionally excludes standardized implementation details, focusing instead on the algorithmic approach rather than specific model implementations. Pascal and Dale shared findings that good algorithm design often outweighs the benefits of advanced embeddings in schema search, with Dale noting that a lexical search with specific parameters (7-8 and factor 2-3) provided effective results for GraphQL schemas.

### Schema Search Performance Optimization

Pascal explained that schema search and schema introspection both pollute context, but schema search is optimized for single requests while semantic introspection allows multiple turns. Pascal suggested that if the agent harness could support storing schema results in a special context location rather than as normal tool results, it would significantly improve performance. The team discussed naming conventions for the Q parameter, with Dale explaining the reasoning behind choosing Q over curry, and the group generally approved of the naming choice.

### Schema Handling Implementation Discussion

Pascal and Mark discussed the ideal implementation of schema handling in their system, emphasizing the preference for in-memory processing over file writing when possible. They clarified that schema search is not a GraphQL request or response but a separate endpoint, distinct from standard GraphQL introspection. Mark suggested adding full HTTP request and response examples for clarity in the documentation.

### GraphQL Schema Implementation Discussion

Pascal suggested using plain text initially for the GraphQL schema implementation, with the possibility of evolving to a more specific format in future releases. Dale and the team discussed the need to define a new media type for this use case and considered integrating it into the HTTP specification as an optional feature. The group debated whether omitting the "q" parameter in the URL should return the full schema, with Pascal clarifying that the specification should guarantee the returned schema is sufficient for building a valid operation, though not necessarily one that answers the specific question.

### Client-Side Query System Implementation

The team discussed implementing a query system where reasoning happens on the client side rather than the server to avoid additional server work and leverage agent intelligence. Pascal recommended limiting requests to one per query to prevent agents from making multiple unnecessary requests when schemas cannot fully answer questions. The group also addressed how clients can discover service support for this functionality, determining that without a skill, it's impossible to detect support, and with a skill, clients can check for GraphQL endpoint availability through capabilities checks.

### Semantic Search GraphQL Implementation

The team discussed implementing semantic search capabilities in GraphQL, focusing on using HTTP status codes like 204 to indicate when a schema supports semantic search. Pascal explained how the capabilities API could be used to provide clients with information about supported search endpoints, noting that these endpoints don't need to be on the same server as the schema service. The group agreed to add this topic to the November AI working group agenda for further discussion about where to place the specification, potentially in the GraphQL over HTTP specification or as part of the AI working group.
